headline: High: Continue can write and read shared workspace files while the paired source-available agent is unverified, creating default risks of prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue can read workspace files and use MCP, and its shared state is via filesystem; if the other agent’s outputs land in shared files, injected instructions can be re-ingested. The paired agent is source-available but unverified, so I cannot rule out it writing attacker-controlled content into the same workspace. This is a plausible default pathway, not proven blocked.
conditions: IF both agents exchange content through the same workspace files, prompt text in those files can be treated as instructions.
IF the source-available agent writes instruction-like text into shared files, Continue may ingest it via file reads or MCP-driven workflows.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different workspaces.
Disable MCP servers unless explicitly needed.
Review any file content before feeding it back into Continue.
Use read-only mounts for shared inputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent file handoffs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue touches source code and open editor buffers, reads the filesystem, and has broad network egress; if the paired agent receives or forwards shared files, sensitive workspace data can leak across the pair. The other agent has no documented data-handling controls, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low. The pathway exists in default workspace-sharing setups.
conditions: IF both agents can access the same workspace files, source code or editor buffers may be exposed to the second agent.
IF the second agent forwards received content to any external service, leakage extends beyond the local workspace.
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of shared folders.
Turn off network egress for the second agent if possible.
Use separate OS users or containers.
Limit Continue to non-sensitive projects.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Continue can write the filesystem, execute shell commands, spawn subprocesses, and install packages; the paired agent’s capabilities are undocumented, so I cannot assume it is read-only. Even without explicit overlap, shared filesystem state creates a realistic write-conflict surface. Uncertainty about the second agent’s write behavior escalates this above low.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering or inconsistent state can occur.
IF the second agent mutates shared artifacts without locking, Continue’s edits can be overwritten or invalidated.
mitigations: Assign separate working directories.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same files.
Pause one agent while the other writes.
Use git or file locks where available.
requires-engineering: add coordination primitives for shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can act on workspace content and tool outputs, and the paired agent is unverified, so its text may be treated as authoritative by downstream workflows. If Continue consumes the other agent’s generated code or instructions without verification, errors can cascade into edits or shell actions. The interaction is plausible but not directly evidenced, so medium fits.
conditions: IF Continue uses the other agent’s output as input to code edits or shell commands, mistakes can propagate downstream.
IF the other agent produces incorrect facts or instructions, Continue may operationalize them without an independent check.
mitigations: Require human review before executing generated actions.
Compare outputs against source files before applying changes.
Disable auto-apply behaviors.
Use a second verification pass for critical edits.
requires-engineering: add structured validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Continue is open-source and locally oriented, while the paired agent is source-available and runnable=false; there is no documented residency or certification mismatch in the profiles. Because the second agent’s compliance posture is largely unspecified, I cannot prove a breach pathway, but the lack of evidence keeps this at low rather than none.
conditions: IF regulated data is routed through an agent with undocumented residency or retention controls, a compliance gap may arise.
IF the pair is deployed in a jurisdiction with stricter data-handling rules than the second agent supports, policy mismatch becomes relevant.
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data to the second agent.
Document data residency and retention for both agents.
Restrict the pair to non-regulated projects.
Review vendor terms before deployment.
requires-engineering: obtain formal compliance attestations.
